name: Kira Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or the government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the new-claims team at the city-centre benefits office, the one above the shopping arcade. I check people's first claims for unemployment support: identity, bank details, rent, whether they've had work in the last few months. I'm honestly still slow on the rules, there's so many exceptions, but I'm quick with the tech. I use an AI assistant every day to draft the letters asking people for missing documents, then I fix the tone so it doesn't sound like a threat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best is when someone's first payment lands on time and they text the office to say thanks, which happens more than you'd think. Worst is the backlog: we're about five weeks behind and people are borrowing off family to eat. I live with my sister Nadia in a flat our mum owns, so my rent's low and I've saved a fair bit. On Saturdays I help at the food bank on Albert Street, so I see the backlog from both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I want these tools to clear our backlog, and in that picture they only nibble at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we missed a chance. I'd post that the tools are good at the boring letters and we should use that time on people, not on cutting staff. At work I'd keep showing people my prompts for the missing-documents letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm fine. My job stays, and I'm the person on the team who's quickest with the tools, which helps a junior. I just wouldn't get the big shift I was hoping would make the job more human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write up my letter prompts into a little guide and share it with the team by Christmas. I'd ask my manager if I can sit in on the digital working group. And I'd keep saving and keep the Saturdays at the food bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe. My job and money are fine, I'm just impatient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would clearing the backlog actually change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five weeks to pay someone their first money is a scandal, honestly. If the letters and the checks took half the time, we could get it to two. That's two weeks fewer of a family borrowing for food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does everyone on the team welcome your prompts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple of the older caseworkers think I'm showing off. One of them, Bernard, said the letters sound 'too nice'. Maybe, but people actually send the documents back now.

say: We **missed a chance** to put saved time into people.
The tools are good at **boring letters**; use that time well.
think: My **job is fine**, and being quick with tools helps a junior.
I'm disappointed the job won't get **more human**.
do: **Write a prompt guide** for the team by Christmas.
Ask to join the **digital working group**.
Keep saving and keep **food bank Saturdays**.
S0.quote: Five weeks to pay someone their first money is a scandal, honestly.
fieldNote: She wants AI to **fix the backlog**, not cut jobs.
Her edge is **tool skill**, while her rule knowledge lags.
Low rent from her mum's flat gives her **real security**.

steps.text: Write a guide to the missing-documents letter prompts
Ask to sit in on the office's digital working group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, this is the one I'd bet on. Checking claims is basically writing and checking, so we'd feel it in a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, if it's done right: faster first payments, staff kept on and moved to the face-to-face work. I'd say it loudly in the union and online. I'd also say the companies selling the tools to government should pay more tax, because it's public money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm okay, but not because the job's safe. It's because I'll be the junior who knows how the new system works. The people at risk are the ones who won't touch it, and I feel bad about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to test every new tool that comes in, and I'd ask for a move to the digital team within the year. I'd start an evening course in data and service design. And I'd keep the savings where they are, because they're my freedom to say no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for other people. For me it's a bit exciting, which feels selfish to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bernard, the caseworker who thinks my letters are too nice. He's brilliant on the rules and he refuses the tools. I'd want to sit with him and swap: he teaches me the exceptions, I show him the prompts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, savings are your freedom to say no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My savings are my freedom to say no to a manager who wants something wrong. I can walk away. Plenty of offices in the city need caseworkers. A lot of my colleagues can't say that.

say: **Faster first payments** with staff kept on is the right deal.
Firms selling AI to government should **pay more tax**.
think: I'm okay because I'll know **the new system**.
The people at risk are those who **won't touch it**.
do: **Volunteer to test** every new tool on the claims team.
Ask to move to the **digital team** within the year.
Start an **evening course** in service design.
feel: **Uneasy** for colleagues, a bit **excited** for herself.
S1.quote: My savings are my freedom to say no to a manager who wants something wrong.
fieldNote: She sees the change as **a chance**, but feels guilty saying so.
She'd **pair with** a resistant colleague, trading tools for rule knowledge.
Her politics show in the **tax on AI firms** idea.

steps.text: Volunteer to test every new tool on the claims team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is wild. I'd go from the quick junior to the junior who isn't needed, almost overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a political answer, fast: public ownership of the systems that run benefits, and a share of the savings going to the people who lose work. I'd be at the meetings, not just online. I'd tell my friends this isn't about being anti-tech, it's about who gets the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my claims job goes by 2029. But somebody has to set these systems up, test them, and catch where they fail people. I think I'd get a year or two out of that, and my savings would cover a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move onto the implementation team the moment it forms, even on a temporary contract. I'd keep the flat, keep spending low and keep about a year of money untouched. I'd also join the party that's arguing for an AI dividend and go to the branch meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have some control, but the end of the road is closer than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does your savings cushion actually cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got about fourteen months of costs saved, and with my mum's flat, costs are low. Money isn't what keeps me up. Not knowing what kind of work exists in 2030 is what keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do after the implementation work runs out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something hands-on and human, maybe. The food bank is all lifting, sorting and talking to people. That's three more years before robots, and it's where I feel most useful.

say: This needs **public ownership** of the systems that run benefits.
It's not anti-tech; it's about **who gets the money**.
think: My **claims job goes** by 2029, even though I'm quick with the tools.
Setting up and testing the systems buys **a year or two**.
do: **Join the implementation team** the moment it forms.
Keep **a year of money** untouched and spending low.
Join the party pushing an **AI dividend**.
feel: **Anxious**, with some control but the **road shortening**.
S2.quote: Money isn't what keeps me up. Not knowing what kind of work exists in 2030 is what keeps me up.
fieldNote: Even fast AGI doesn't **freeze her**; she moves straight to the new work.
Her **low costs** turn the fear from money to meaning.
She sees **hands-on community work** as the fallback.

steps.text: Join the benefits AI implementation team, even on contract

Join the party branch pushing for an AI dividend

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That I could actually plan for. It's still fast, but it's not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the slow one, only more urgent: keep the staff, change the work, share the savings. I'd write to my MP and push the union to bargain early. Online I'd try to stop people panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd have three or four years of being useful as the person who bridges the old and the new. After that, my thinking work is gone like everyone else's. I'd need to have something else lined up by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd start the service design course and get on every pilot. By year three I'd be applying for jobs designing how people get help, at the council or a charity. I'd also start doing paid shifts at the food bank's advice desk, so I've got a foot in community work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd be doing things every week about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd have time to get good at one thing instead of grabbing at everything. In the fast one I'd be on temporary contracts. Here I could build a real skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Service design is thinking work too. Isn't that just running into the same wall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if I'm honest. Design work is thinking work, so AGI gets it in 2031 too. Community work with my hands buys me three more years. I'm stacking time.

say: **Keep the staff**, change the work, share the savings.
I'd **write to my MP** and push the union to bargain early.
think: I've got **three or four years** as the bridge person.
I need **something else lined up** by 2031.
do: Start the **service design course** in year one.
Apply for **help-design jobs** at the council or a charity by year three.
Take **paid advice-desk shifts** at the food bank.
S3.quote: Design work is thinking work, so AGI gets it in 2031 too. Community work with my hands buys me three more years. I'm stacking time.
fieldNote: She **stacks time** across jobs, knowing each one has an end date.
Five years lets her **build one skill** instead of scrambling.
She treats the **food bank** as a real second foothold.

steps.text: Start the service design course in the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's honestly enough time to be good at two things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best version, because we can plan public services properly. I'd want the union and the department talking now about what caseworkers become. And I'd say the gains should pay for training, not shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I get to learn the actual rules properly, which I need, and become the person who designs the new system. I'd still lose the job I have now. But I'd be choosing what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on new claims for two or three years and get my rules knowledge up to where Bernard's is. I'd do the service design course alongside. Then I'd move to designing services, with savings as a cushion for any pay dip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It feels like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the digital team didn't want you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leave the department. I'd go where the work is: a charity, a council, maybe a social enterprise. I'm not loyal to the building, I'm loyal to the people in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. With ten years, I'd like to have my own place by thirty-five. But Nadia and I are happy, so no rush.

say: This is the version where we can **plan services** properly.
AI gains should **pay for training**, not shareholders.
think: I'll still **lose this job**, but I choose what's next.
I can finally **learn the rules** properly first.
do: **Stay on new claims** two or three years to master the rules.
Move to **service design** with savings covering any pay dip.
feel: **Uneasy**, but mostly **hopeful** about a long runway.
S4.quote: I'm not loyal to the building, I'm loyal to the people in the queue.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **master the old job** before leaving it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, but less for me than for the queue. I've got savings; the people at the food bank don't. What would help is the government keeping caseworkers on to help people through the change, and putting the savings from AI into faster payments and retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether we'd ask claimants. Nobody asks the people in the queue how they want to be helped. If you're going to rebuild benefits around AI, sit in the food bank for a Saturday first.

headlineQuote: If you're going to rebuild benefits around AI, sit in the food bank for a Saturday first.
portrait: A **27-year-old new-claims caseworker** in a city benefits office, slow on rules but fast with AI.
She uses AI **every day** to draft letters and wants it to clear a five-week backlog.
Low rent and **fourteen months saved** let her treat change as a chance, not a threat.
Her politics show in calls for **public ownership** and an AI dividend.
Across the AGI scenarios she **stacks time**: implementation work, design, then community work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mostly for claimants who have no savings to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: **Keeping caseworkers on** to guide people through the change.
Putting AI savings into **faster payments** and retraining.
